extracted.intended_audience: general readers, researchers, journalists, and students interested in the Anti-Defamation League, antisemitism definitions, and related controversies
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes the standards, definitions, and procedural practices described in an encyclopedic article about the Anti-Defamation League (ADL), including how the ADL and others define antisemitism, what signals/gestures they label, and historical tactics the organization used to combat defamation.

rubrics_metrics.name: ADL definition of a Nazi salute
rubrics_metrics.description: The ADL defines a Nazi salute as "raising an outstretched right arm with the palm down."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as the organization's descriptive standard when assessing gestures (e.g., controversy over Elon Musk's salute). The article records disagreement about whether particular gestures meet this definition (ADL called Musk's gesture "an awkward gesture" not a Nazi salute; other groups and individuals described it as an "unambiguous" or "Heil Hitler" salute).

rubrics_metrics.name: IHRA definition of antisemitism (and ADL promotion)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ADL and many Jewish establishment organizations have promoted adoption of the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA) definition of antisemitism, which includes examples that treat certain criticisms of Israel and forms of anti‑Zionism as antisemitic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page notes ADL's advocacy for governments to adopt IHRA and records criticism that using IHRA conflates criticism of Israel with antisemitism and can chill legitimate speech; critics argue this shift changes how antisemitism is identified and investigated in public institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: OCR Title VI guidance enabling campus antisemitism investigations (2004)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 2004 policy guidance letter from Kenneth L. Marcus (Assistant Secretary for OCR) empowered Office for Civil Rights staff for the first time to investigate complaints under Title VI alleging pervasive antisemitism on college campuses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Described in the article as a "game-changing" policy that allowed allegations of pervasive antisemitism (including rearticulations tying anti‑Zionism to antisemitism) to be examined under federal civil‑rights law; used historically in debates over campus speech and discrimination investigations.

rubrics_metrics.name: The 'New Antisemitism' typology (Forster & Epstein, ADL 1974)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ADL-published book The New Anti-Semitism (1974) stitched together a list/typology of antisemitic threats, broadening the concept to include right‑wing threats alongside threats 'emanating from The USSR, Western Europe, Latin America,' and groups labelled as 'the Radical Left,' 'Arabs and Pro‑Arabs,' and Black Americans — and including anti‑Zionism within this frame.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as a conceptual rubric used to identify and classify forms of antisemitism beyond traditional far‑right antisemitism; critics argue this typology expanded the label of antisemitism to encompass various political critiques of Israel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical ADL anti‑defamation tactics (procedural practices)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tactics described in ADL historical materials: request the right to inspect proposed performances before staging; organize boycotts of theaters if prior censorship refused; protests to editors; correct defamations via subsequent articles; appeal to patrons and advertisers for cooperation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are procedural response options the ADL proposed or used historically to combat perceived public defamation; the article frames them as examples of applying organizational pressure (including financial pressure) to address defamatory portrayals.

rubrics_metrics.name: ADL naming/listing of extremists (guides and glossaries)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ADL produces resources (e.g., a 'Who's Who' guide of alt‑right/alt‑lite extremists and an extremism glossary) that identify and name organizations and movements as extremist (examples mentioned include Turning Point USA and Christian Identity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page records that inclusion in ADL lists/glossaries can prompt backlash; it notes an instance where an ADL extremism glossary entry provoked right‑wing backlash and was removed. The article does not provide the internal criteria ADL uses for inclusion, but it treats the act of naming as a de facto standard with political consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: ADL revision of definitions (example: racism definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ADL revised its definition of racism after criticism that the prior definition was 'so narrow' (reported by CNN), indicating the organization updates definitional standards in response to critique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article cites this as evidence that the ADL's definitional standards (e.g., for 'racism' or 'antisemitism') can change over time; details of the revised wording are not provided on the page excerpt.
